title: Choosing a Hub license
description: Distinguish a hosted subscription from licensing a self-hosted deployment.

chapters.title: A subscription for the hosted service

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Imagine a fictional team connecting a few Agents for the first time. They want to try Hub without operating the platform themselves. What should they understand about licensing?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The guide separates the hosted service from a self-hosted installation. For the hosted route, you register an account and choose a subscription. Features and allowances can depend on that subscription, so check the current offering for your actual needs.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: So the useful question isn't simply how many cameras we own?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Right. Think about bandwidth, retention, live viewing and the capabilities you need. The guide links to the product information for those choices. Avoid treating an old example or a spoken overview as a current price list.

chapters.title: A license for your own installation

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Now suppose the same team needs to run Hub in its own infrastructure. Is the hosted account subscription the installation key?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: No. The self-hosted route uses a license key configured for that deployment through the Helm chart. It is a different operational arrangement: your organisation runs the installation rather than using the hosted platform.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should the team do before ordering anything?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Decide which deployment model fits, list the capabilities and scale you need, and confirm the current licensing terms through the linked product information. Keep the actual key private and follow the installation guide for configuration.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Hosted subscription or self-hosted license: choose the model first, then check the current terms. That's the key distinction.

editorialStyle.tone: A short, high-level introduction for a first-time listener. Explain why the topic matters, build one mental model, and suggest one next action. Sound like two colleagues, not a narrated manual.
editorialStyle.scope: Aim for four to five minutes and roughly 500-550 spoken words. Use one fictional example and four short chapters. Leave identifiers, form limits, configuration, migration mechanics, and troubleshooting checklists in the linked guide. Keep essential caveats as practical consequences.
editorialStyle.humour: Optional: one or two brief, relevant light moments are enough. Prefer a relatable analogy over a separate joke. Never pad the overview with banter.
editorialStyle.reactions: Use occasional short, natural responses such as 'Oh, that makes sense' or 'Wait, so...' followed by a real question. Avoid repetitive praise, canned agreement, and filler.
editorialStyle.laughter: Optional: at most one or two light reactions such as 'Ha, fair point.' Never insert [laughs], SSML, or repeated ha-ha strings. These are spoken reactions, not a guarantee of genuine laughter from the current speech engine.
editorialStyle.intonation: Write real questions with question marks, use contractions, alternate short and longer sentences, and make contrasts explicit. Let punctuation and sentence rhythm suggest curiosity, surprise, and emphasis. Avoid all-caps shouting, excessive exclamation marks, and artificial pause tags.
editorialStyle.guardrails: Keep technical claims source-backed. Never mock the listener, joke about real victims, minimize security or data-loss risks, or let humour replace an explanation. Personality is optional; accuracy and clarity are not.
